description: We are a team of Computer Engineering students participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are passionate about technology, science, innovation, and problem-solving. We are looking for enthusiastic people from different backgrounds who want to collaborate and contribute with skills in programming, hardware, AI, data, analysis, design, astronomy, communication, and more. No previous experience is required-just creativity, curiosity, and a willingness to learn and work together.
summary:
NEXXUS: Earth in Motion is an interactive web app that turns NISAR radar data into something anyone can explore. On a 3D globe, each analyzed scene is a clickable marker. Opening one shows the satellite’s repeat passes in a before-and-after slider, a change map that measures in km² where the radar signal fell and where it rose, and whether the change is a documented event with sources or a seasonal change interpreted by the team. Two viewing levels, Simple and Data, go from plain-language results to HH/HV polarization views and measurements in dB, and an AI assistant answers questions about each scene.

This matters most when nothing else can see. In the Taquari Valley flood of July 2026 in Brazil, cloud hid the valley from optical satellites for more than two weeks missing the peak; NISAR measured about 53 km² of new open water the night after the crest. NISAR data is open, but it comes as large calibrated files that few people can read. Nexxus, open source, turns them into an answer anyone can check: where the surface changed, by how much, and how far the measurement can be trusted.
details:
Project Repository: https://github.com/Gabrielhyds/Hackathon-Nasa-apps-challenge-2026.git

What it does and how it works

  • A 3D globe shows the Earth’s surface with a clickable marker on each analyzed SAR scene (eleven at present). For any other place, the app lists the real NISAR passes over that point, with the radar track, the date of the last pass and an estimate of the next one. The sky behind the globe is also real: 15,500 stars from ESA’s Hipparcos catalogue, placed where they actually are behind the Earth at the moment the page is opened.
  • Clicking a marker opens the scene’s passes (two or more repeat passes of the satellite over that area), with before-and-after images, the analysis results and a description of the event. For the Taquari flood, the optical image from the day of the pass shows only cloud, and the radar appears through it.
  • A change map compares any two passes of a scene, paints where the radar signal fell (amber) and where it rose (ice blue) beyond a threshold, and reports the area of each side in km². A sensitivity control moves the threshold, and a play button steps through the passes one at a time.
  • Each scene states what it rests on: a documented event with its sources (two floods and an earthquake sequence) or a seasonal change, interpreted by the team from the images.
  • The depth of the data depends on the viewing level the user chooses:
    • Simple (general public and classrooms): before-and-after comparison, result and short description, the sources that document the event, and a guided activity that explains how the NISAR radar works by asking the user to predict the change and then check it.
    • Data (researchers): HH and HV polarization views and detailed analysis, with a histogram of the change in dB, the signal in dB under the pointer and the origin of each pass.
  • A radar lab adds three tools: a flood gauge for the Taquari Valley (new open water in each of 8 NISAR passes, checked against river levels), a fringe ruler that counts fringes in a real interferogram of the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes, and a pulse compression simulation.
  • A built-in AI agent answers questions about the scenes in plain language, using only fact cards verified by the team, and attaches sources and a caveat to each answer.

Key findings

  • Taquari Valley, Brazil (flood of 22 July 2026). On the night after the crest, NISAR measured about 53 km² of new open water (49 to 56 km², depending on the water threshold), against 0.3 to 1.6 km² in the reference passes. Four days later it was about 5 km². The river gauge at Lajeado read 24.7 m on the day of the crest.
  • Radar was the only view. There was no clear optical view of the valley between 15 July and 1 August, and the Sentinel-1 passes behind the OPERA water maps (13 and 25 July) missed the peak.
  • Chókwè, Mozambique (Limpopo flood, January 2026). The change map separates two effects: about 173 km² got darker, the flood strip along the river, and about 3,450 km² got brighter, the surrounding ground.
  • Northern Venezuela (earthquakes of 24 June 2026). Along the same line, the interferogram that spans the earthquakes shows 4.7 fringes, against 0.7 in the pair before them. Each fringe is about 12 cm of change in the distance to the satellite. The app counts fringes and stops there: it does not convert them into ground displacement.
  • Several seasonal scenes (Campinas, Kalimantan, Lábrea) barely change between the two dates, and the app says so.

Benefits

  • It makes NISAR data accessible beyond remote sensing specialists.
  • It shows change through direct visual comparison and a measured area, not raw data.
  • It combines images, charts and written explanations, so users can start with a quick visual answer and go deeper to verify it.
  • One tool serves the general public, schools and professionals, in English and Portuguese.
  • It is open source, so others can reuse and improve it.

Intended impact

The project aims to help scientists, resource managers, educators, decision makers and the public understand changes in the Earth’s surface (floods, earthquakes, changes in ice and seasonal change) and communicate them clearly, with better-informed decisions as a result.

Looking ahead: NISAR revisits the same ground every 12 days, in any weather, with open data. With a longer archive the same method could follow a flood from rise to retreat, tell flooded cropland from floodwater, track planting and harvest cycles, and watch forest loss under cloud. Interferometry adds ground motion: earthquakes, subsidence and glacier flow.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NISAR L2 GCOV (calibrated backscatter, HH and HV) and GUNW (interferograms) from NASA Earthdata; NISAR pass catalogue from NASA CMR; globe imagery, cloud cover and optical imagery from NASA GIBS; OPERA DSWx-S1 water maps from NASA JPL.
  • Front end: React, TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre GL for the 3D globe.
  • Back end and processing: NestJS API in TypeScript; Python scripts that read the NISAR HDF5 files.
  • AI agent: Python and FastAPI, with Google Gemini restricted to fact cards verified by the team.
  • Hosting: Docker on a cloud virtual machine, behind Cloudflare, at https://nexxus.earth
  • License: MIT

Creativity

Nexxus goes beyond displaying radar images. It is a layered experience: a globe, a marker for each story, two levels of explanation, charts from the simplest to radar signal analysis, and a conversational agent. In the Under cloud mode, the screen shows what an optical satellite saw on the day of the flood, only cloud, and the radar image sweeps in through it. A specialist dataset becomes something anyone can explore, with the scientific detail still there for those who need it.

Factors considered

  • Accessibility for non-specialists without losing scientific rigour.
  • Clear communication of what changed and why.
  • The physics behind the signal. Calm open water acts as a mirror and reflects the pulse away from the satellite, so flooded ground turns dark. New water is counted where HH fell by 3 dB or more against a low-water pass of the same orbit and ended below −12 dB. Wet soil does the opposite: water raises its dielectric constant, more energy returns and the ground brightens, which is the interpretation given to the bright area around the Limpopo.
  • Polarizations. HH responds most to smooth surfaces and to water, so it is the one used for floods. HV comes mostly from volume scattering in vegetation, so it is the one to watch for forest and crop change. The app lets the user switch between them on every scene that has both.
  • Validity of the analysis: the flood measurement is checked on screen against river gauge readings, the OPERA DSWx-S1 water map (NASA JPL, derived from ESA’s Sentinel-1) and the optical record. Each scene shows its sources and a caveat on how the signal can mislead.
  • Current limitations: the app covers eleven analyzed scenes, most of them with two passes, and “new open water” is not the total flooded area, because water under trees or between buildings does not show up this way. Next steps include analyzing more scenes and separating flooded cropland from floodwater, so the Taquari series can extend beyond July.
  • Open-source reuse.

Use of AI

  • In the product: the Ask tab uses Google Gemini at run time, restricted to fact cards verified by the team; an answer with a number, date or scene that is not in the cards is rejected.
  • Code: written with AI coding assistants, mostly Claude Code (Anthropic), under the direction of the team, who reviewed and ran the result.
  • Text: the project summary, project description, and demo video script were drafted with ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic), then reviewed and edited by the team.
  • Logo: the NEXXUS logo, wordmark and icon were generated with ChatGPT image generation and are marked “SI-generated” wherever they appear. The project name was chosen by the team without AI.
  • Demo video: edited and assembled with Claude (Anthropic) from real recordings of the app, with narration by a team member; it carries the mark "SI-generated video edit".
  • Everything else: radar and optical images are real satellite data. No other image or music is AI-generated, and the project uses no NASA logo or mission identifier.
